etymology: Traces back to the Proto-Indo-European first-person root *eǵ(h₂); Old Church Slavonic азъ shifted through regular sound changes into the modern form.
commonMistakes: Unlike English I, it's lowercase everywhere, even sentence-initial it's just normal. In casual speech it's often dropped since the verb ending already shows the subject, but formal writing keeps it.

etymology: Goes back to the Proto-Indo-European negator *ne, the common Slavic negation particle.
commonMistakes: Placed directly before the verb (no do-support like English). Double negation is standard (ничего не знаю = 'I don't know anything'), the opposite of English grammar norms.

etymology: From Proto-Indo-European *tuH, cognate with English thou and Latin tu.
commonMistakes: Using the informal ты with strangers or elders reads as rude; default to вы until invited to switch.

etymology: Traces to the Proto-Indo-European interrogative root *kʷod, a distant cousin of English what.
commonMistakes: Spelled что but pronounced closer to 'shto' — don't read чт literally (a classic чт→шт pronunciation exception).

etymology: The neuter form of the demonstrative этот, which became an independent pointing word.
commonMistakes: Learners overuse it as a catch-all translation of English 'it', but это is fundamentally 'this' — it doesn't automatically cover every dummy-subject 'it' construction.

etymology: Goes back to Proto-Indo-European *h₁en, cognate with English in.
commonMistakes: Case governance trips learners up: destination/motion takes accusative (в школу), location/staying takes prepositional (в школе).

etymology: The basic coordinating conjunction shared across Slavic languages, carried over unchanged from Old Church Slavonic.
commonMistakes: Overused where а (contrastive 'and/but') would fit better for drawing a contrast between two clauses.

etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European demonstrative root *h₁ono.
commonMistakes: Unlike Japanese 'he', он also refers to inanimate masculine nouns (e.g. стол 'table') — not limited to people.

aspectUsage: Imperfective-only verb. Its 'partner' побыть ('to stay for a while') is a delimitative, not a true aspectual pair. Usually dropped entirely in the present tense (Я студент. has no быть) — the one exception is possessive у меня есть, where есть survives.
etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European existential root *bʰuH-, cognate with Latin fui and English be.
commonMistakes: Dutifully inserting есть in every present-tense sentence (it's normally omitted outside the possessive construction).

etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European first-person plural *wei-.
commonMistakes: Its case forms (нас/нам/нами) resemble ты's and вы's closely enough to confuse beginners.

etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European second-person plural *yu-; its polite singular use spread from 18th-century French influence.
commonMistakes: Even when addressing one person politely, verbs and past-tense adjectives stay plural (Вы правы., not Вы прав.).

etymology: Traces to the Proto-Indo-European comitative root *ḱom, a distant cousin of Latin cum.
commonMistakes: 'With' takes instrumental (с другом), but 'since/from' takes genitive (с утра = 'since morning') — the governed case shifts with meaning.

etymology: Goes back to Proto-Indo-European *h₃en, cognate with English on.
commonMistakes: Like в, destination (accusative) vs. location (prepositional) governs the case; also certain nouns (почта, работа, вокзал) idiomatically take на instead of в.

etymology: Split off as the feminine form from the same demonstrative root as он.
commonMistakes: Also used for inanimate feminine nouns (машина 'car'), just like он for masculine ones.

etymology: A derivative of the Proto-Indo-European interrogative/relative root *kʷo-.
commonMistakes: Doubles as an exclamation marker (Как хорошо! 'how wonderful!') and a question word (Как дела? 'how are you?') — context decides which.

etymology: The regularly-formed plural of он.
commonMistakes: Case forms gain an н- after a preposition (у них) — easy to drop by mistake.

aspectUsage: Imperfective; its perfective partner смочь marks a single successful instance of 'managing to'. As a modal of ability it has no normal imperative.
etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European ability root *magʰ-, cognate with English might.
commonMistakes: Confused with уметь (a learned skill). мочь is situational possibility; уметь is acquired competence.

etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European deictic particle *do, an old affirmative response word.
commonMistakes: Tacked onto the end of a statement it means 'right?' (Хорошо, да?) — don't mistake every да for a plain 'yes'.

etymology: The plural nominative form of весь ('all/every'), which became an independent pronoun meaning 'everyone'.
commonMistakes: Easily confused with всё ('everything') — they look and sound almost identical but все is for people, всё for things.

etymology: The neuter singular form of весь, independently lexicalized as 'everything'.
commonMistakes: Mixed up with все (people vs. things); also note the ё carries its own distinct 'yo' sound.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root denoting proximity.
commonMistakes: The possessive construction 'у меня есть' is distinctly Russian — beginners keep looking for a separate verb 'to have' that doesn't exist here.

etymology: A contraction of не + есть, now a standalone negative/absence word.
commonMistakes: Besides plain 'no', it also expresses absence ('there is no' — У меня нет денег.) — the meaning shifts with context.

etymology: The genitive/accusative form of он, repurposed as an indeclinable possessive determiner.
commonMistakes: As a possessive ('his') it never changes for gender or number — unlike мой and other true possessives.

aspectUsage: Imperfective. узнать ('to come to know' — find out, get acquainted) is a derived action verb with a shifted meaning, not a strict aspectual pair.
etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European cognition root *ǵneh₃-, cognate with English know.
commonMistakes: Mistaking узнать for simply 'the past of знать' — it actually means 'find out/come to know', a different event.

etymology: From the deictic root *tok, functionally matching English so across the Slavic languages.
commonMistakes: Its filler/discourse use (Так, слушай. 'So, listen.') sounds odd if you only know the 'so/thus' textbook meaning.

etymology: An adversative coordinating conjunction from an old Slavic contrast root.
commonMistakes: Distinguish from а: а draws a plain contrast ('this is X, that is Y'), while но marks a stronger 'but/however'.

etymology: Traces to a Proto-Indo-European contrastive particle, common across Slavic.
commonMistakes: Its sentence-opening use 'and what about...?' (А ты как?) feels abrupt if you don't know this conversational pattern.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European preposition root marking proximity/relation.
commonMistakes: Shifts to об before a vowel-initial word (об этом) — easy to forget. Governs the prepositional case.

etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European first-person possessive root *moi-; inflects for gender and number like an adjective.
commonMistakes: Must agree in gender/number/case with the noun it modifies (мой дом / моя книга / моё окно).

aspectUsage: Imperfective; perfective захотеть marks the sudden onset of a desire ('suddenly wanted'). As a desire verb it has no normal imperative.
etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European volition root, functionally parallel to (but not cognate with) English want.
commonMistakes: The irregular stem alternation (хоч- in the singular, хот- in the plural) gets misremembered as a regular conjugation.

etymology: A fusion of the demonstrative этъ with the intensifying particle ото.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse the inflecting этот (agrees with its noun) with the invariant это ('this/it').

etymology: A fusion of есть + ли (the question particle) into a conditional conjunction.
commonMistakes: Hypotheticals require 'если бы + past tense' — a different construction from English if-clauses.

aspectUsage: Perfective; its imperfective partner говорить covers ongoing/repeated speaking. сказать marks a single completed utterance.
etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root for speech/telling.
commonMistakes: Mixing up the pair: using говорил where сказал is needed for a single past utterance.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root meaning 'beyond/behind'.
commonMistakes: Accusative (motion/duration: за час 'in an hour') vs. instrumental (location: за столом 'behind the table') — the case shifts with meaning.

etymology: A contracted old aorist form of быть, now a particle that builds the subjunctive/conditional.
commonMistakes: The subjunctive is formed with бы + a PAST-tense verb even when talking about present or future hypotheticals — unlike English.

etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European demonstrative root *to-, cognate with English that.
commonMistakes: Ignoring the distance contrast: этот ('this', near) vs. тот ('that', far).

aspectUsage: Imperfective; perfective подумать marks a bounded act of 'thinking it over for a bit'.
etymology: Said to derive from the Proto-Indo-European thought root *dʰeu-.
commonMistakes: 'Think about X' governs о + prepositional — putting the object in the accusative instead is a common slip.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European directional root.
commonMistakes: Governs the dative (к другу 'to a friend's place') — easy to forget. Becomes ко before certain consonant clusters (ко мне).

etymology: A fusion of что + бы into a purpose/intent conjunction.
commonMistakes: The purpose clause's verb must be past tense (different subject) or infinitive (same subject) — never a plain present/future form.

etymology: From Old Church Slavonic чловѣкъ; the deeper origin is debated.
commonMistakes: Its plural is NOT человеки — it's the suppletive люди (registered as its own separate headword, see LINGO-022).

aspectUsage: Imperfective 'to eat'. Perfective съесть marks 'finishing eating (all of) something'. A different word entirely from the existential/possessive есть (from быть) and the affirmative есть — same spelling, unrelated meaning.
etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European eating root *h₁ed-, cognate with English eat.
commonMistakes: Confusing this есть with the invariant existential/possessive есть — context is the only disambiguator.

etymology: From the same possessive root as мой, split off as the second-person form.
commonMistakes: Using informal твой with someone you'd otherwise address as вы is impolite — use ваш for the formal register.

etymology: Traces to the Proto-Indo-European emphatic particle *ǵʰe.
commonMistakes: It's multi-purpose (emphasis, impatience, sameness) — translating it mechanically as a single fixed word misses the nuance.

etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European reflexive possessive root *swe-.
commonMistakes: A reflexive possessive that tracks the SUBJECT of the clause regardless of person (Я взял свою книгу. = 'I took my [own] book') — distinct from мой/твой/etc.

etymology: The adverbial form of простой ('simple'), whose meaning broadened into a colloquial filler/intensifier.
commonMistakes: Beyond its literal 'simply', it's also a common intensifier meaning 'really/just' (Это просто ужасно! 'That's just awful!') — easy to miss.

etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European separative root *h₁eǵʰs.
commonMistakes: Blurring из (originating from inside something) with от (starting from a nearby point).

etymology: An old adverb expressing continuation/addition ('still, more').
commonMistakes: Mixing up ещё не ('not yet') with уже ('already') — they're nearly opposite in meaning.

aspectUsage: Imperfective; perfective сказать marks a single utterance. говорить also covers ongoing conversation and language ability ('speak Russian').
etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European speech root, suppletive with сказать for its aspect pair (different roots).
commonMistakes: 'Speak Russian' needs по-русски (preposition по + adverbial form) — a literal говорить русский is wrong.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European totality root — a universal quantifier/determiner.
commonMistakes: Inflects for gender/number/case (весь/вся/всё/все) — don't confuse with the invariant pronoun всё ('everything').

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root expressing purpose/benefit.
commonMistakes: Governs the genitive (для друга 'for a friend') — easy to forget. Also confused with чтобы (для + noun vs. чтобы + verb clause).

etymology: A fusion of сей ('this') + час ('hour/moment') meaning 'this moment'.
commonMistakes: Blurs with теперь ('now, as opposed to before' — implies a change of state); сейчас is just plain 'now/right away'.

etymology: An old Slavic interjection-like filler particle.
commonMistakes: A multi-purpose filler (prompting, hesitation, surprise) — pinning it to one textbook meaning makes your speech sound stilted.

etymology: A time conjunction derived from a Proto-Indo-European interrogative/relative root.
commonMistakes: Doubles as the question word 'when' and the conjunction 'when (that)' — context determines which.

etymology: The third-person singular of мочь, independently lexicalized as a parenthetical adverb 'maybe'.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse the inflected verb form with the standalone adverbial use (может = short for может быть).

etymology: The adverbial/predicative form of хороший.
commonMistakes: Also functions as an agreement response ('alright, OK') — missing this conversational use feels off.

etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European interrogative root *kʷo-, a distant cousin of English who.
commonMistakes: Grammatically always masculine singular (Кто пришёл? takes a masculine past-tense verb), regardless of the actual gender of the person meant.

etymology: Said to derive from сей ('this') + место ('place').
commonMistakes: Barely distinguishable from the colloquial тут in everyday use — здесь just reads slightly more neutral/written.

etymology: Derived from так ('so/thus') as a demonstrative determiner.
commonMistakes: Forgetting it inflects for gender/number/case (такой/такая/такое/такие).

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European preposition root marking distribution/'along'.
commonMistakes: Governs several different cases depending on meaning (dative by default, accusative for distributive sense, prepositional for 'after') — easy to misapply.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root for 'companion'; masculine noun.
commonMistakes: Its plural друзья is irregular and unpredictable from the singular (this entry covers singular forms only).

etymology: An old interrogative pronoun that became the relative pronoun, equivalent to English which.
commonMistakes: The double agreement rule trips learners up: it matches its antecedent in gender/number but takes its case from its role inside the relative clause.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root for 'season/opportune time'; masculine noun.
commonMistakes: After a number, the genitive plural isn't годов but the suppletive лет (пять лет = 'five years').

etymology: The neuter singular of тот, also used as a standalone demonstrative/connective element.
commonMistakes: Its use introducing the consequence of 'если' ('if... then') is easy to miss, making complex sentences hard to parse.

etymology: Developed from тот + a limiting particle into the adverb 'only'.
commonMistakes: Its position shifts the focus of meaning (Только я знаю. 'Only I know' vs. Я знаю только это. 'I only know this') — word order matters.

aspectUsage: Perfective; its imperfective partner делать covers the ongoing/repeated act of 'doing'. сделать marks one completed act.
etymology: делать with the perfectivizing prefix с- attached.
commonMistakes: Using сделал for a past habitual or still-in-progress action, where делал is the correct choice.

etymology: The genitive/accusative plural of она (via они), repurposed as a possessive determiner.
commonMistakes: Like его, it's indeclinable as a possessive — a frequent slip is trying to inflect it.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European numeral root; an unusual numeral that inflects for gender (один/одна/одно).
commonMistakes: Overlooking that it inflects like an adjective (один/одна/одно/одни) despite being a numeral.

etymology: From Old Church Slavonic хорошии ('splendid').
commonMistakes: Its comparative isn't a regular хорошийше-type form but the suppletive лучше ('better').

aspectUsage: Imperfective; perfective сделать marks a single completed act. делать covers ongoing/repeated/habitual doing.
etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European action root *dʰeh₁-.
commonMistakes: Aspect mix-up with сделать — using делал for a single completed past act.

etymology: A fusion of во + тот (demonstrative) into a pointing particle 'here/there'.
commonMistakes: Beyond pointing at a physical thing, it's also a discourse marker for 'that's why' (Вот почему я ушёл.) — a use learners often miss.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European separative root.
commonMistakes: Blurred with из (от = starting from a nearby point/person, из = from inside something).

etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European dwelling root *domh₂-, cognate with Latin domus; masculine noun.
commonMistakes: Separate from the case form доме are the adverbs дома ('at home') and домой ('homeward') — easy to mix up with the prepositional phrase в доме.

etymology: The second-person plural/polite possessive, derived from вы.
commonMistakes: Like твой, forgetting it inflects for gender/number/case (ваш/ваша/ваше/ваши).

etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European reflexive root *swe-; a special pronoun with no nominative form.
commonMistakes: Has no nominative case at all (only used in oblique cases) — trying to use it as a subject is a category error.

aspectUsage: Imperfective; perfective увидеть marks the instant of 'catching sight of' something. As a perception verb it has no normal imperative (use смотри for 'look').
etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European vision root *weid-, distantly related to English wit.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the д→ж consonant shift in the first person (вижу), and regularizing it to a nonexistent 'виду'.

etymology: Said to derive from раб ('servant') via a diminutive, shifting to mean 'child'; masculine noun.
commonMistakes: Its plural isn't ребёнки but the suppletive дети — the same irregular pattern as человек/люди.

etymology: A fusion of по + the dative interrogative чему, forming the 'why' adverb.
commonMistakes: Confused with зачем ('for what purpose') — почему asks for a cause, зачем for a goal.

etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European action root *dʰeh₁-, same root as делать; neuter noun.
commonMistakes: The plural дела leans toward an abstract 'affairs/business' sense distinct from the singular.

etymology: Of disputed dialectal origin; a colloquial masculine noun for a young man/boyfriend (soft declension).
commonMistakes: A soft-declension noun, so its case endings differ from hard-declension masculines (genitive парня, instrumental парнем).

etymology: Of disputed origin (possibly linked to око 'eye'); an intensifying adverb 'very'.
commonMistakes: Mixed up with слишком ('too much', excess) — очень is plain intensification.

etymology: Said to derive from an old comparative form, meaning 'already'.
commonMistakes: Mixing up ещё не ('not yet') with уже ('already') — nearly opposite meanings.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root for rotation/cycle; neuter noun, the representative of the irregular -мя noun class.
commonMistakes: Mistaking the irregular -мя declension (an -ен- infix in all oblique forms) for a regular pattern.

etymology: The first-person plural possessive, derived from мы.
commonMistakes: Forgetting gender/number/case agreement (наш/наша/наше/наши), same as мой and твой.

etymology: From a root meaning 'servant/slave' (раб), which shifted to mean 'labor'; feminine noun.
commonMistakes: 'At work' idiomatically takes на, not в — using в работе for the location is a common slip.

etymology: A contraction of спаси + бог ('God save [you]'), a thanking interjection.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that what you're thankful for is marked with за + accusative (Спасибо за помощь.).

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European disjunctive conjunction root.
commonMistakes: Its sentence-final confirming use (Ты придёшь, или? 'You're coming, or?') feels abrupt if you don't know this pattern.

etymology: From Old Church Slavonic боліи ('greater'), a comparative that became the base form.
commonMistakes: Its comparative isn't a regular form but the suppletive больше ('bigger').

etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European father root *atta; masculine noun.
commonMistakes: The stem vowel drops in every oblique case (the 'fleeting vowel' pattern: отец → отца).

aspectUsage: Imperfective; perfective дать marks one completed act of giving. давать is for repeated/habitual giving.
etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European giving root *deh₃-, cognate with Latin dare.
commonMistakes: The imperative давай/давайте is an extremely common 'let's...' suggestion formula — learning only the literal 'give' meaning misses this entirely.

etymology: From baby talk, a near-universal word for 'mother'; feminine noun.
commonMistakes: Not distinguishing it from the more neutral/formal мать (мама carries warmth/familiarity) can sound out of place.

etymology: From the adjective ладный ('harmonious'), an agreement response 'alright'.
commonMistakes: Beyond plain agreement, it often carries a shade of resignation ('fine, whatever') — easy to miss.

etymology: From the demonstrative root то-, a place adverb meaning 'there'.
commonMistakes: Confusing там ('there', location) with туда ('to there', direction) — a location/direction distinction many adverbs make.

etymology: The neuter short-form of the adjective нужный ('necessary'), fixed as a predicative.
commonMistakes: It doesn't conjugate like a verb — it's an invariant predicative, and the person who needs something is marked with the dative (Мне нужно идти.).

aspectUsage: Imperfective, unidirectional (motion in one direction). Perfective пойти marks the start of the motion. For back-and-forth/repeated motion use ходить (its own headword).
etymology: From the Proto-Indo-European motion root *h₁ei-; the past tense шёл is a suppletive form from a different root entirely.
commonMistakes: Not realizing the past-tense шёл/шла/шло/шли shares no root with the present-tense иду series, so hunting for a regular pattern is futile.

etymology: A fusion of сей ('this') + the genitive of день ('day'), meaning 'today'.
commonMistakes: The spelling hides день, but it's pronounced closer to 'sevodnya' — the г becomes a в sound, a pattern shared with words like его.

etymology: A derivative of the Proto-Indo-European location root *kʷo-.
commonMistakes: Mixed up with куда ('where to', direction) — где only asks about static location.

etymology: The instrumental form of the interrogative что, lexicalized as the comparative conjunction.
commonMistakes: The 'than' after a comparative (чем) shouldn't be treated like English 'that'.

etymology: The genitive form of ничто ('nothing'), independently lexicalized.
commonMistakes: Its use as a reassurance ('it's fine, no big deal' — Ничего, бывает.) is easy to miss if you only know the literal 'nothing'.

etymology: The suppletive comparative of большой, fixed as its own adverb.
commonMistakes: The 'больше не' ('no longer') emphatic-negative pattern gets misread as plain quantity comparison instead.

etymology: From a Proto-Indo-European root marking an endpoint.
commonMistakes: Governs the genitive (до дома 'up to the house') — easy to forget outside the fixed phrase до свидания.
